abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are promising for healthcare question answering, yet adapting them with sensitive clinical data can induce unintended memorization and privacy leakage. We present MedDP, an efficient privacy-budgeted adaptation framework that delivers an auditable utility-privacy trade-off under ($\epsilon,\delta$)-differential privacy. Our method, MedDP, applies DP-SGD only to low-rank adapter parameters while freezing the base model, using per-example gradient clipping and calibrated Gaussian noise to enable explicit privacy accounting with minimal compute and memory overhead. To improve the stability of noisy optimization, we introduce Adaptive Clipping (AC) that updates the clipping bound online via a quantile-based rule with momentum. To avoid spending additional privacy budget on late-stage accuracy degradation, we further propose Budget-Aware (BA) checkpoint selection, which chooses the best checkpoint on the training trajectory subject to a target budget $\epsilon _\rm{max}$, without re-training. For privacy evaluation, we adopt a canary-based suite and emphasize canary negative log-likelihood (NLL) as a more sensitive memorization signal than hit-rate. Experiments on public medical QA benchmarks derived from MedQA and MedMCQA, together with synthetic canary auditing, characterize a clear privacy-utility frontier in a controlled evaluation setting. Non-private LoRA improves average accuracy but increases memorization signals, whereas privacy-budgeted training mitigates memorization while maintaining stable performance under explicit privacy accounting.

titulo: Development of a Meta-Question Enhanced Retrieval-Augmented Generation Model and Its Application in Dermatology

abstract: RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation) provides a solution for enhancing domain-specific knowledge in large language models by interacting with external information. RAG functions similarly to a search engine, retrieving the most relevant knowledge or related conversation history to the user's query. It then combines this with the original query to create a detailed prompt, guiding the model to generate accurate outputs. However, traditional RAG methods match short queries with long texts in the knowledge base, leading to mismatched results despite apparent similarities due to length discrepancies. To address this issue, we propose the MQ-RAG (Meta Questions Retrieval Augmented Generation) method, a question-answer pair-based approach built upon RAG. The key difference in MQ-RAG lies in the retrieval and recall content: it uses a database of Meta Questions, which are pairs of questions and corresponding answers. When using MQ-RAG, queries are matched with Meta Questions to retrieve the most relevant answers, ensuring high compatibility between the query and the retrieved content. For evaluation, 100 multiple-choice questions from the Dermatology and Venereology Medical Licensing Examination database were selected. Results showed that, using Qwen2-7b and Qwen2-72b as base models, MQ-RAG improved accuracy by 17.14% and 2.27%, respectively, compared to traditional RAG. Our MQ-RAG method demonstrated higher accuracy across both large and small parameter models, with particularly significant improvements in smaller models.

titulo: Instruction Tuning and CoT Prompting for Contextual Medical QA with LLMs
autores: C. Le; Z. Gong; C. Wang; H. Ni; P. Li; X. Chen

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown great potential in medical question answering (MedQA), yet adapting them to biomedical reasoning remains challenging due to domain-specific complexity and limited supervision. In this work, we study how prompt design and lightweight fine-tuning affect the performance of open-source LLMs on PubMedQA, a benchmark for multiple-choice biomedical questions. We focus on two widely used prompting strategies-standard instruction prompts and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompts-and apply QLoRA for parameter-efficient instruction tuning. Across multiple model families and sizes, our experiments show that CoT prompting alone can improve reasoning in zero-shot settings, while instruction tuning significantly boosts accuracy. However, fine-tuning on CoT prompts does not universally enhance performance and may even degrade it for certain larger models. abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), particularly Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), is widely used to adapt large language models (LLMs) to specialized downstream domains. During training, sequence-origin domain labels supervise the tokenwise gate outputs, while an asymmetric loss mask prevents general-domain language-modeling losses from directly updating the LoRA parameters. During inference, the learned gate suppresses unnecessary LoRA contributions on general-domain inputs. Under a predefined equivalence margin of ±1.0 percentage points, TDG-LoRA is statistically equivalent to standard LoRA on GSM8K and MedQA and to the corresponding base model reference on post-adaptation Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU). On Llama-3.1-8B, TDG-LoRA achieves 58.92% accuracy on GSM8K while retaining 65.18% on MMLU, corresponding to a decrease of only 0.05 percentage points from the base model. Their structured decision pathways can be used for retrieval to enhance clinical decision making. However, these methods often face challenges in understanding the structure of decision trees and accurately extracting the complete content of tree nodes, leading to noise in the extracted trees and ultimately impacting their effectiveness in clinical decision support system. To this end, in this paper, we propose a novel decision tree extraction framework, including two stages. In the first stage, we propose to use the If-Else pseudocode to represent the decision tree structure and design specific constraints on format and content to guide the LLM in generating outputs. In the second stage, we introduce a novel node-filling strategy called PlanSelect to match the extracted triplets with sub-sentences in the generated pseudocode, including four reasoning steps: observation, plan, action, and answer. abstract: In recent years, large language models (LLMs) have achieved state-of-the-art performance across diverse natural language processing (NLP) tasks, yet persistent concerns remain about their robustness, reliability, and ability to generalize under adversarial or domain-shifted conditions. Conventional evaluation methods often depend on static benchmarks and costly human annotation, limiting scalability and reproducibility. This work introduces an autonomous evaluation framework that unifies benchmark-driven testing with automated adversarial probing for systematic, end-to-end assessment of LLM robustness. The framework is instantiated using the DeepSeek-7B-Chat and Mistral-7B-Instruct models and evaluated across three distinct QA benchmarks—SciQ (scientific), MedQA (medical), and FinQA (financial reasoning)—under both clean and perturbed conditions. Results reveal high robustness in the medical domain (ΔF1 ≈ 0) and minor but consistent degradation in financial reasoning (ΔF1 ≈ –0.0033), highlighting domain-dependent sensitivity to linguistic and numerical perturbations. Comparative analysis between DeepSeek and Mistral indicates consistent robustness trends across architectures, underscoring the generality of the proposed evaluation protocol. Overall, the framework captures semantic consistency, factual accuracy, and error resilience while reducing evaluation time from weeks to hours and improving coverage by over 30 % relative to human-only baselines. Beyond empirical gains, it establishes a reproducible, domain-and model-agnostic methodology for robustness assessment, advancing standardized and scalable evaluation practices for reliable LLM deployment in high-stakes domains such as medicine and finance.

abstract: Medical multiple-choice question (MCQ) answering requires specialized domain knowledge, multi-step clinical reasoning, and ability to discriminate among closely related distractor options. Current large language models (LLMs) frequently exhibit hallucinations, inconsistent reasoning patterns, and unstable performance when confronted with complex biomedical scenarios. This study introduces a structured multiagent framework integrating Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with Model Context Protocol (MCP) to enhance accuracy and reliability in medical reasoning tasks. The proposed architecture employs an administrator agent that performs domain-specific task routing and coordinates five specialized medical agents-Physiology, Pathology, Clinical Medicine, Treatment and Pharmacology, and Public Health-integrating their outputs through weighted consensus for final answer selection. Critically, this study demonstrates that knowledge database quality significantly outweighs quantity in RAG systems: curating high-quality question subsets from knowledge data yields substantially greater performance gains than utilizing entire unfiltered knowledge datasets. These findings establish that domain specialization, structured agent collaboration, and strategic data curation collectively enhance both accuracy and interpretability in medical reasoning systems, offering practical pathway for deploying reliable clinical decision support without computationally expensive model fine-tuning.

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for medical question answering, where understanding when to trust their outputs is critical. Recent work has shown that increasing the sampling temperature substantially raises textual diversity while having little effect on accuracy, suggesting that surface-level variability is a weak proxy for reliability. In this paper, we investigate whether this independence between temperature and correctness also holds when variability is measured in the semantic embedding space. We evaluate three LLMs, including general-purpose and medically specialized models, on MedQA and the medical subset of MMLU. For each question and temperature, we generate multiple stochastic responses, embed them with a sentence transformer, and compute the total convex hull area of clustered embeddings as a geometric measure of semantic dispersion. Across models and datasets, higher temperatures consistently increase semantic spread, yet accuracy remains largely unchanged. This extends prior findings from textual to semantic-manifold variability and reveals a form of semantic stability: LLMs tend to preserve their answer choice even as their expressed reasoning becomes more diverse. These findings support human-centered AI by linking uncertainty to human oversight in medical decisions. They also highlight limitations of diversity-based uncertainty measures and motivate future work on cluster-based analyses of LLM reasoning.

The model is evaluated using the MedQA USMLE benchmark and a collection of prompts created from MIMIC III data, as well as by comparing the performance of the system against a general purpose LLM and a fine tuned medical LLM. abstract: Medical diagnosis using large language models (LLMs) like GPT-4 has shown significant promise with advancements such as MedPrompt, which leverages chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning and choice-shuffling ensembles. However, the exponential growth in computational complexity with an increasing number of ensembles limits the scalability of such systems. This study re-implements MedPrompt from scratch and introduces a distributed framework using Ray to address these limitations. By parallelizing CoT reasoning, our approach achieves substantial reductions in processing time, enabling the use of more than 20 ensembles while maintaining state-of-the-art diagnostic accuracy of 90.6% on the MedQA dataset. Preliminary results indicate that our distributed system reduces processing time from over 4,800 seconds to less than 400 seconds for 20 ensembles.

titulo: Advancing Healthcare with Large Language Models: Techniques and Application
autores: Z. Hu; Z. Peng; Z. Bi; Q. Shen; Z. Liu; J. Lou; X. Luo
venue: IEEE/CAA Journal of Automatica Sinica
keywords: Measurement; Analytical models; Costs; Reviews; Large language models; Retrieval augmented generation; Medical services; Benchmark testing; Faces; Application; healthcare; large language models (LLMs); medicine; techniques
abstract: As the costs of global healthcare systems continue to rise, large language models (LLMs) have emerged as a promising technology with vast potential and wide-ranging applications in the medical field. We provide a detailed overview of the lifecycle of medical LLMs, encompassing three key stages: get, refine, and use, aimed at assisting healthcare practitioners and patients in utilizing these models more effectively. We also summarize the currently widely used medical evaluation benchmarks, analyzing their advantages and limitations. Furthermore, we conduct a comparative analysis of specialized medical LLMs on benchmarks such as MedQA, PubMedQA, MMLU-MED, and MedM-CQA, revealing that methods like retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enable smaller models to outperform larger ones by effectively integrating external medical knowledge. This review provides a reference for medical professionals to evaluate LLM capabilities and inspires the development of more effective benchmarking methods. Additionally, we showcase practical applications of medical LLMs in clinical, research, and educational settings, providing healthcare workers with valuable resources. Finally, we identify current challenges faced by medical LLMs and present outlooks for future technological advancements, aiming to inspire users to explore new ways to address existing issues. This review serves as an entry point for interested clinicians, helping them determine whether and how to integrate LLM technology into healthcare for the benefit of patients and practitioners.

titulo: An Iterative Multi-Agent Analysis for Automated Evaluation in NLG Tasks
autores: H. Alhawasi; R. Shan; A. Youssef
venue: 2025 IEEE 7th International Conference on Cognitive Machine Intelligence (CogMI)
keywords: Natural language generation; Iterative methods; Machine intelligence; Convergence; Multi-Agent Analysis; Similarity Evaluation; Classification; NLG; QA; Summarization
abstract: Evaluating the similarity of generated text and reference text in natural language generation (NLG) remains a challenge. Current automatic evaluation methods have limitations and fall short of expectations. Therefore, we propose an iterative multi-agent analysis system to enhance the evaluation of similarity between ground-truth and generated answers. The system has a Task Performer (Stage 1) for initial evaluation, Multi-Agent Analysis (Stage 2), where specialized analysis agents iteratively re-evaluate outputs, and a Convergence Checker (Stage 3) that determines consensus, with an Arbiter invoked when convergence is not reached. We implement our method in three architectures: (1) Architecture One employs all three stages with an Arbiter; (2) Architecture Two is limited to stages 2 and 3; and (3) Architecture Three is like Architecture One but without the Arbiter – if no convergence, the Task Performer’s final answer is the final output. We evaluated our system on four datasets (Open-QA, SummEval, MedQA, and ChatLaw) under three different LLM implementation scenarios (uniform, closed-source, and small open-source). The results show that our system performs better than a standalone LLM baseline and is significantly closer to human evaluation levels.

titulo: RoboMed: On-Premise Medical Assistance Leveraging Large Language Models in Robotics
autores: A. Basit; K. Hussain; M. A. Hanif; M. Shafique
venue: 2024 18th International Conference on Control, Automation, Robotics and Vision (ICARCV)

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are revolutionizing numerous domains with their remarkable natural language processing (NLP) capabilities, attracting significant interest and widespread adoption. However, deploying LLMs in resource-constrained environments, such as edge computing and robotics systems without server infrastructure, while also aiming to minimize latency, presents significant challenges. Another challenge lies in delivering medical assistance to remote areas with limited healthcare facilities and infrastructure. To address this, we introduce RoboMed, an on-premise healthcare robot that utilizes compact versions of large language models (tiny-LLMs) integrated with LangChain as its backbone. Moreover, it incorporates automatic speech recognition (ASR) models for user interface, enabling efficient, edge-based preliminary medical diagnostics and support. RoboMed employs model optimizations to achieve minimal memory footprint and reduced latency during inference on embedded edge devices. The training process optimization involves low-rank adaptation (LoRA), which reduces the model's complexity without significantly impacting its performance. For fine-tuning, the LLM is trained on a diverse medical dataset compiled from online health forums, clinical case studies, and a distilled medicine corpus. This fine-tuning process utilizes reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) to further enhance its domain-specific capabilities. The system is deployed on Nvidia Jetson development board and achieves 78% accuracy in medical consultations and scores 56 in USMLE benchmark, enabling an resource-efficient healthcare assistance robot that alleviates privacy concerns due to edge-based deployment, thereby empowering the community.

titulo: CRITIC-RAG: Knowledge-Augmented Large Language Models With Verified Retrieval for Improved Medical Reasoning
autores: J. Li; L. Lu; Y. Miao; Y. Tian; J. Li
venue: IEEE Journal of Biomedical and Health Informatics
keywords: Modeling; Retrieval augmented generation; Large language models; Cognition; Cognitive systems; Filtering; Filters; Labeling; Grounding; Accuracy; Large language models; Retrieval-augmented generation; Factual verification; Hallucination; Instruction tuning
abstract: While retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) presents a promising solution for enhancing large language models (LLMs) in question answering (QA), particularly in knowledge-intensive domains like medicine, it continues to face challenges related to factual consistency and reasoning reliability. To address this challenge, we propose CRITIC-RAG, a verification-enhanced framework that integrates a small-size, instruction-tuned verifier throughout the RAG pipeline. Our method incorporates selective retrieval, evidence filtering, structured reasoning through self-consistency, and groundedness verification. This approach enhances the accurate utilization of external knowledge while reducing spurious generations. Comprehensive experiments across five medical QA benchmarks and multiple LLM backbones confirm the framework's broad applicability and plug-and-play adaptability. For instance, CRITIC-RAG improves accuracy from 41.3% to 48.8% on MedQA and boosts BERTScore from 68.1% to 74.4% on MedicationQA using LLaMA-3. Ablation studies further reveal that evidence filtering and structured reasoning are especially critical to robust performance. Case studies and retrieval analyses, including improvements in entailment-based similarity scores and factual accuracy, demonstrate how each stage of verification jointly contributes to generating more accurate, evidence-grounded responses. Overall, our work highlights verification as a key mechanism for enhancing trustworthiness in knowledge-intensive medical QA, a capability that is increasingly important for clinical decision support and other real-world healthcare applications.

titulo: FedLoRA-C: Communication-Efficient Federated Fine-Tuning of Large Language Models via Selective Layer Compression
autores: L. R. Gandikota; V. Jegathesan; C. D. R. Reddy
venue: 2026 2nd International Conference on Artificial Intelligence Systems (AIS)
keywords: Modeling; LoRa; Quantization (signal); Accuracy; Tuning; Sensitivity; Manuals; Federated learning; Ranking (statistics); Training; Federated Learning; Large Language Models; LoRA; Communication Efficiency; Distributed AI; Edge AI; NLP Fine-Tuning; Non-IID Data
abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) in federated settings presents a fundamental tension: the gradients and adapter parameters that encode task-specific knowledge are large enough to make communication the primary bottleneck, yet aggressive compression risks convergence degradation. This paper introduces FedLoRA-C, a communication-efficient framework for federated fine-tuning that combines Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) with a novel selective layer compression (SLC) strategy. SLC identifies and prioritizes the subset of transformer layers contributing disproportionately to task-specific adaptation using a gradient-based layer sensitivity scoring function, transmitting only the top-K% of layers at full precision while applying 4-bit quantization to the remainder. We evaluate FedLoRA-C on four NLP benchmarks (SST-2, MNLI, SQuAD 1.1, MedQA) across heterogeneous federated configurations simulating IID and non-IID data distributions with 10-100 clients. FedLoRA-C achieves within 1.4% of centralized fine-tuning accuracy while reducing per-round communication cost by 67.3% compared to standard FedAvg with LoRA. Ablation studies confirm that sensitivity-scored layer selection outperforms random selection by 2.2% at identical communication cost, with the advantage increasing under higher data heterogeneity. These results demonstrate that high-fidelity federated LLM fine-tuning is achievable under realistic bandwidth constraints.

titulo: Enhancing Medical Question Answering via a Multi-Agent Debate Framework
autores: D. Lu; V. Jiang; S. Wang; M. Zhu; S. Zhai

abstract: Despite large language models (LLMs) showing strong capabilities in general medical question answering, they still struggle with multi-domain knowledge coverage, consistent reasoning, and preventing hallucination in complex clinical conditions. This paper introduces a two-stage Classification—Debate Multi-Agent Framework that improves reasoning consistency, accuracy, and interpretability. In the first stage, the system performs MeSH-guided domain classification, routing medical multiple-choice questions into multiple LLM-based “medical specialist” agents, each of which has expertise in a specific medical subfield, such as anatomy, organism, diseases, etc. In the second stage, domain-specific agents independently generate answers and engage in structured debate rounds upon shared history, with the final decision determined by consensus or majority voting. Experiments on MedQA and MedMCQA demonstrate consistent accuracy gains across all model configurations. Results further show that fine-grained domain classification improves reasoning alignment, and that output format also significantly affects performance. Without requiring additional fine-tuning, retrieval augmentation, or complex pipelines, the proposed lightweight framework outperforms single-model baselines and several existing multi-agent systems, highlighting the effectiveness of integrating domain-aware classification with structured debate.

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) achieve state-of-the-art performance on natural language processing tasks but impose substantial computational demands that limit accessibility in academic and resource-constrained environments. This paper presents a comprehensive empirical study comparing three fine-tuning strategies—4-bit QLoRA, 16-bit LoRA, and 16-bit Full Fine-Tuning—applied to Facebook’s OPT-1.3B on the IMDb sentiment classification benchmark. Experiments are conducted with 2,500 training and 2,500 test samples, class-wise evaluation metrics, proper latency methodology with GPU synchronization (torch.cuda.synchronize), and actual power measurement via nvidia-smi. A LoRA rank ablation study ($r \in\{4,8,16\}$) further characterises the accuracy–efficiency trade-off under 4-bit quantization. Results show that 4-bit QLoRA achieves competitive accuracy with only 0.32% trainable parameters, reducing peak GPU memory by $\approx 75 \%$ relative to 16-bit Full Fine-Tuning while incurring a negligible accuracy penalty. The study provides reproducible, hardware-aware insights for deploying parameter-efficient LLMs on consumer-grade GPUs.

This paper focuses on evaluating the performance of various LLMs—Llama-2-7b, T5, Bart, and Pegasus—specifically fine-tuned on the CNN Daily dataset of news articles. abstract: The automation of code review activities, a long-standing pursuit in software engineering, has been primarily addressed by numerous domain-specific pre-trained models. Despite their success, these models frequently demand extensive resources for pre-training from scratch. In contrast, Large Language Models (LLMs) provide an intriguing alternative, given their remarkable capabilities when supplemented with domain-specific knowledge. However, their potential for automating code review tasks remains largely unexplored.In response to this research gap, we present LLaMA-Reviewer, an innovative framework that leverages the capabilities of LLaMA, a popular LLM, in the realm of code review. Mindful of resource constraints, this framework employs parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods, delivering high performance while using less than 1% of trainable parameters.An extensive evaluation of LLaMA-Reviewer is conducted on two diverse, publicly available datasets. Notably, even with the smallest LLaMA base model consisting of 6.7B parameters and a limited number of tuning epochs, LLaMA-Reviewer equals the performance of existing code-review-focused models.The ablation experiments provide insights into the influence of various fine-tuning process components, including input representation, instruction tuning, and different PEFT methods. abstract: Grading handwritten programming assignments for “Algorithm Design and Analysis” is burdensome and suffers from inconsistent scores. titulo: From Billions to Bits: A Taxonomy and Survey of Optimization Methods for Large Language Models
autores: A. Choudhary; A. Arasamangalam; S. Kemtur; S. Madihal; S. Mucchandi; T. Bulla; U. Kulkarni
venue: 2025 IEEE Conference on Engineering Informatics (ICEI)
keywords: Modeling; Quantization (signal); Memory; Optimization; Accuracy; LoRa; Tuning; Printing; Ranking (statistics); Artificial intelligence; Large Language Models; Model Quantization; Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning(PEFT); Medical Artificial Intelligence; LLaMA Architecture; Edge Computing; Healthcare Applications; Model Compression
abstract: Physician shortages, rising patient numbers, and urgent clinical judgments are putting increasing strain on health-care systems around the world, especially in settings with limited resources and little access to advanced diagnostic assistance. Large Language Models (LLMs) automate medical documentation, assisting in patient triage, and supporting diagnostic workflows, yet their deployment remains impractical: a 70 billion parameter model requires 140 GB of memory in full precision, inference latency exceeds clinical acceptability on standard hardware, and privacy regulations crutial on-premise deployment that most facilities cannot support. This survey addresses the deployment gap by analyzing optimization techniques that make LLaMA models available for real-world medical applications. We evaluate three quantization methods (GPTQ, AWQ, NF4) that compress model weights to 4-bit precision, and three parameter-efficient fine-tuning approaches (LoRA, QLoRA, AdaLoRA) that enable domain adaptation by training only 0.01-0.1% of model parameters. Experimental evaluation on WikiText-2 and MMLU benchmarks demonstrates that quantization achieves 3.5-4× memory reduction with 94-99% accuracy retention across models from 7B to 65B parameters, while PEFT methods maintain 95-99% of full fine-tuning performance. Combined optimization enables a 70B model to operate within 48 GB memory with sub-2-second inference on consumer GPUs—practical for clinical deployment. Analysis of PMC-LLaMA shows that LoRA fine-tuning improved MedQA-USMLE accuracy from 36.1% to 56.4% using only 0.036% trainable parameters. While identifying important gaps in domain-specific quantization, regulatory validation frameworks, and uncertainty quantification that need more research, our findings demonstrate that the strategic integration of quantization and parameter-efficient fine-tuning increases access to advanced medical AI by allowing resource-constrained facilities to deploy models previously only available to well-funded research institutions.

titulo: How Can Quantum Deep Learning Improve Large Language Models?
autores: E. J. Roh; H. Ahn; S. Y. -C. Chen; S. Park; J. Kim

abstract: The rapid progress of large language models (LLMs) has transformed natural language processing, yet the challenge of efficient adaptation remains unresolved. Full fine-tuning achieves strong performance but imposes prohibitive computational and memory costs. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) strategies, such as low-rank adaptation (LoRA), Prefix tuning, and sparse low-rank adaptation (SoRA), address this issue by reducing trainable parameters while maintaining competitive accuracy. However, these methods often encounter limitations in scalability, stability, and generalization across diverse tasks. Recent advances in quantum deep learning introduce novel opportunities through quantum-inspired encoding and parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs). In particular, the quantum-amplitude embedded adaptation (QAA) framework demonstrates expressive model updates with minimal overhead. This paper presents a systematic survey and comparative analysis of conventional PEFT methods and QAA. The analysis demonstrates trade-offs in convergence, efficiency, and representational capacity, while providing insight into the potential of quantum approaches for future LLM adaptation.

titulo: MLX vs MPS on Apple Silicon: A Comparative Empirical Study of LoRA Fine-Tuning Performance for LLMs
autores: A. T. Kabakuş
venue: 2026 10th International Artificial Intelligence and Data Processing Symposium (IDAP)
keywords: Modeling; Training; Memory; LoRa; Timing; Tuning; Silicon; Printing; Large language models; Machine learning; large language model; fine-tuning; LoRA; Apple Silicon; MLX; MPS
abstract: Fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs) on Apple Silicon devices has gained increasing attention due to their unified memory architecture and integrated GPU capabilities. Two relevant software backends for this purpose are PyTorch with Metal Performance Shaders (MPS) and Apple’s native MLX framework. This paper presents a controlled empirical comparison of both backends for Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning of the TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0 model on an Apple A18 Pro chip. Using a dataset of 200 prompt-response samples derived from the Alpaca Cleaned dataset, training was performed for 200 steps under matched experimental conditions, including a LoRA rank of eight, a LoRA scaling factor of 16, a dropout rate of 0.05, a learning rate of $\mathbf{1} \times \mathbf{1 0}^{-\mathbf{4}}$, three warmup steps, a maximum gradient norm of 1.0, and a maximum sequence length of 128 tokens. Experimental results show that MLX completes the training process in 52.15 s, compared with 4,809.89 s for MPS, corresponding to an approximately 92.2-fold speedup in training time. MLX achieves a throughput of 3.835 samples/s, whereas MPS achieves 0.0416 samples/s. Despite this substantial difference in execution time, both backends exhibit broadly similar loss behavior, with average losses of 1.626 for MLX and 1.759 for MPS, and final losses of 1.281 and 1.340, respectively. The observed results indicate that MLX provides substantially higher execution efficiency for the evaluated LoRA workload while exhibiting broadly similar loss dynamics to MPS. Gradient norms exhibit broadly similar magnitudes, although their variability differs between the two backends. These findings suggest that MLX can provide a substantial performance advantage over PyTorch MPS for LoRA fine-tuning on Apple Silicon under the evaluated experimental configuration, particularly in time-sensitive scenarios.

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have rapidly advanced task automation by enabling high-quality natural language understanding, reasoning, and multi-modal interaction across domains such as software development, healthcare, customer service, and scientific discovery. Despite their transformative potential, challenges such as high computational cost, domain adaptation, safety, and robust error handling remain significant barriers to practical deployment. Recent research has addressed these issues through techniques including parameter-efficient fine-tuning, retrieval-augmented generation, domain-specific pretraining, tool integration, and multi-agent orchestration frameworks, which collectively improve scalability, adaptability, and reliability. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of state-of-the-art approaches to LLM-driven task automation, systematically categorizing methods by optimization strategy, integration architecture, and application scenario. Implementation challenges are further analyzed, and emerging solutions are reviewed that aim to balance performance, efficiency, and trustworthiness. This review provides a synthesized perspective on how LLMs are evolving toward robust, context-aware automation systems suitable for real-world deployment.

titulo: An Empirical Study of App Review Classification Using Large Language Models
autores: N. Neupane; F. Kamal; M. R. Islam
venue: 2026 IEEE/ACIS 24th International Conference on Software Engineering Research, Management and Applications (SERA)
keywords: Labeling; Modeling; Reviews; Tuning; Poles and zeros; Printing; Testing; Bit error rate; Training; Terminology; Review Classification; Large Language Models; Prompt Engineering; Few-Shot Learning; Fine-tuning; Software Engineering
abstract: App store reviews are a primary signal for software maintenance decisions, yet classifying them reliably remains challenging due to informal language, brevity, and overlapping class boundaries. Large language models (LLMs) offer prompt-based alternatives to supervised classifiers that eliminate annotation costs, but three gaps limit their practical adoption: the effect of prompt structure on classification performance is understudied, evaluation on app review datasets is scarce relative to formal specification corpora, and direct protocol-controlled comparisons between prompting and parameter-efficient fine-tuning are rare. This study addresses all three gaps through a systematic, threephase evaluation. We assess four open-source LLMs-Llama 3 8B/70B, Gemma 3 4B, and Mistral 7B-across three app review datasets (PAN, Maalej, Scalabrino) differing in class granularity and annotation philosophy. Seven structurally distinct prompt templates are compared in a zero-shot exploratory phase, followed by stratified 10-fold cross-validation experiments with shot counts from 0 to 7. The best prompt-based configuration is then compared against QLoRA-fine-tuned Llama 3 8B and four supervised encoder baselines (e.g., RoBERTa). The definitionbased prompt template significantly outperforms all alternatives across every model-dataset combination, with the largest gains on the most fine-grained dataset. Few-shot prompting improves over zero-shot in most conditions, though gains are non-monotonic on datasets with semantically overlapping classes. RoBERTa and QLoRA achieve statistically equivalent performance and both significantly outperform the best prompt-based configuration on two of three datasets, confirming that lightweight fine-tuning provides a measurable and consistent advantage when labeled data is available. When it is not, investing in prompt structure yields more return than scaling model size.

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable efficacy across diverse domains, yet their deployment in sensitive sectors is constrained by data privacy. Federated Learning (FL) offers a promising paradigm for collaborative model training without exposing raw data, while Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) techniques substantially reduce adaptation costs. This survey systematically reviews the integration of FL and PEFT for LLMs, elucidating foundational architectures, mainstream PEFT methodologies, and federated adaptation frameworks. We analyze representative approaches, highlight open challenges, including communication bottlenecks, task and model heterogeneity, parameter anonymity, and adaptation profile misalignment, and propose future research directions. Our work aims to provide a comprehensive reference for advancing privacy-preserving, scalable, and efficient LLM fine-tuning in federated environments.

abstract: This paper presents a parameter-efficient sentiment analysis system for low-resource, code-mixed text using LLaMA 3.1 8B Instruct fine-tuned with Quantized LowRank Adaptation (QLoRA) and 4-bit NF4 quantization. We generated a balanced synthetic dataset (2,520 samples) across entertainment, reviews, and social domains to address data scarcity. Results show $\mathbf{8 0. 2} \pm \mathbf{0. 4 \%}$ accuracy (5 runs), outperforming XLM-R $(79.6 \pm 0.3 \%$, $\mathrm{p}=0.018)$. Real-world validation: ACTSA (77.3%), DravidianCodeMix (75.8%). QLoRA enables training on single consumer GPUs ($<8 ~\text{GB}$), validating efficiency for resource-constrained NLP and framework demonstrates strong generalization capability across domains and maintains balanced precision and recall despite the presence of linguistic variability, transliteration noise, and informal expressions in Telugu-English code-mixed data. The use of synthetic data combined with parameterefficient fine-tuning significantly reduces the dependency on large annotated corpora while preserving contextual understanding. Experimental analysis also confirms that lowbit quantization and adapter-based training improve memory efficiency and scalability without degrading predictive performance. These findings highlight the practicality of deploying large language model-based sentiment systems in real-world low-resource environments, supporting future multilingual NLP applications and scalable adaptation to other under-represented languages.

titulo: Memory Meets Style: Adaptive Fine-Tuning and Contrastive RAG for Smart Code Review Automation

abstract: Building on previous work on parameter-efficient fine-tuning methodologies-specifically Low-Rank Adaptation approach (LoRA) proposed by Edward J. Hu et al., this paper presents an enhanced hybrid framework that combines adaptive QLoRA fine-tuning with a contrastive RAG system that significantly improves both the training efficiency and the inference quality for the code review automation domain. Although existing work done by Sumukh Naveen Aradhya et al. using LoRA, QLoRA and QLoRA with RAG showed promise in offering a good trade-off between memory utilization and output quality, issues still persist in fixed fine-tuning configurations and generic context retrieval. To address these, the proposed method adaptively adjusts the LoRA rank based on input complexity to ensure that optimal capacity is allocated to the model during fine-tuning. This paper also introduces a contrastive retrieval mechanism system that reranks semantically similar code samples based on stylistic similarity. This results in a more realistic and humanlike code review. The framework is evaluated on real-world dataset (more details on the dataset can be found in [11]) with context obtained from Meta's LLaMA 3.2 3B model. The experimental results report up to 55% savings in GPU memory, 20% improvement in CPU efficiency, and decreased entropy in inference output, outperforming prior approaches. The results establish the efficacy of adaptive QLoRA with contrastive RAG as an efficient and viable approach to efficiently automate code review generation using a fine-tuned large language model and also provides a reliable approach to efficiently fine-tune LLMs for any domain.

abstract: The growing complexity of decentralized power systems has the need for intelligent, adaptive tools to support real-time decision-making in microgrid operations. This paper introduces GridLLaMA, a domain-adapted large language model fine-tuned from LLaMA 3.1 (8B) to provide context-aware and precise technically responses across key operational domains Power quality, demand response, voltage stability, and renewable integration. A specialized question-answer (QA) dataset was constructed from 700 technical documents which include Research papers and IEEE standards. The model was fine-tuned using parameter-efficient LoRA methods and filtered through the Nemotron-4 reward model to ensure high-quality instructional responses. Evaluation against a benchmark of general and expert-level questions evaluated via blind review by domain experts demonstrated that GridLLaMA significantly outperforms the base model, achieving 94% accuracy on general questions and 78% on expert-level questions, compared to the base model's 6% and 22%, respectively. The results indicate the potential of domain-specific LLM adaptation for -focused applications and validate GridLLaMA as a scalable tool for intelligent microgrid management.

titulo: An Empirical Study of Exploring the Capabilities of Large Language Models in Code Learning
autores: S. Liu; D. Guo; J. Zhang; W. Ma; Y. Li; Y. Liu
venue: IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering
keywords: Codes; Syntactics; Semantics; Adaptation models; Large language models; Software engineering; Cognition; Analytical models; Predictive models; Java; Large language models; code pre-trained models; probing analysis; parameter-efficient fine-tuning
abstract: Since the advent of ChatGPT, large language models (LLMs) have attracted widespread attention from academia and industry. They have also brought significant changes to software engineering. However, until now, there has been a lack of comprehensive studies comparing LLMs with previous smaller code pre-trained models. To address this gap, we conduct a study in this paper to illustrate the performance of LLMs in different software engineering tasks. Specifically, we select three open-source large language models, CodeGen, LLaMA, and StarCoder, for the research targets, and our study is conducted from four aspects, including code syntax understanding, code semantic reasoning, encoding representation quality, and adaptation performance for different software engineering tasks to compare LLMs with previous code pre-trained models. Four aspects build on each other, forming important components of AI for Software Engineering. We conclude that: (1) Compared with previous smaller pre-trained models like CodeBERT, LLMs exhibit distinct trends in how they learn code syntax or semantics as the number of layers increases. Additionally, mastering code semantics proves to be more challenging, with semantic information usually learned in the final layers; (2) Causal decoder architecture with left-to-right attention masking does not perform well in zero-shot tasks; (3) For classification tasks, the mean vector representation generated by LLMs over a sequence tends to outperform the last token representation in the sequence; (4) Incorporating parameter-efficient fine-tuning techniques into LLMs for downstream tasks can help LLMs achieve better performance than previous code pre-trained models on code generation tasks but may not be optimal in some code understanding tasks; (5) LoRA emerges as a more effective PEFT technique for LLMs in downstream code-related tasks. We hope these findings will better guide future researchers in designing more powerful code models.

abstract: The evaluation of database design quality is essential for assessing undergraduate theses (projects), yet existing approaches suffer from subjective manual reviews and limited rule representation, leading to inconsistent evaluations. This paper proposes a structured evidence-driven framework with expert preference alignment for database design quality assessment. The method constructs knowledge graphs of student and standard designs to generate structured evidence, which is combined with database design information to guide parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large language models. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms text-only and non-fine-tuned baselines on MAE, Pearson, and Acc@1 metrics. titulo: EvoAPR: Enhancing Large Language Models for Automatic Program Repair with Genetic Algorithm and Dynamic LoRA
autores: H. Zhang; Q. Yan; W. Min; C. Zhang; L. Kuang; Y. Xia
venue: 2025 IEEE International Conference on Web Services (ICWS)
keywords: Codes; Fuses; Web services; Large language models; Heuristic algorithms; Computer bugs; Maintenance engineering; Genetics; Software; Indexes; Automatic Program Repair; Project-level Patch Generation; Large Language Models; Genetic Algorithm; Dy-namic LoRA
abstract: Automated Program Repair (APR) aims to automate the patch generation for buggy code and is vital in software devel-opment and maintenance. While large language models (LLMs) excel in various tasks, our empirical study shows they still face challenges in APR. LLMs take infilling templates with different qualities as input, and low-quality templates may misguide LLMs in constantly generating incorrect patches. Additionally, LLMs lack project-specific knowledge and struggle to leverage bug context fully. Therefore, we propose EvoAPR, which integrates the genetic algorithm and dynamic LoRA technique to enhance LLMs for better APR. First, to generate high-quality infilling templates, buggy codes are encoded to genetic representations, and genetic operators and multi-angle evaluation are designed to produce better templates. Then, to effectively utilize bug context, a bug-context-aware LoRA fine-tuning method is proposed to fuse various bug contexts by dynamically activating certain blocks of the LoRA module according to the bug index. Finally, these high-quality infilling templates are fed the fine-tuned LLMs for patch generation. Experimental results demonstrate that EvoAPR significantly improves LLMs' performance, surpassing state-of-the-art methods.

abstract: The rapid development of large language models (LLMs) such as GPT-3, GPT-4, LlaMA, and mBERT has significantly advanced the natural language processing (NLP) field across many widely spoken languages. However, the effectiveness of these LLMs on low-resource languages such as Sinhala remained unexplored. With the scarcity of high-quality data and linguistic resources, fine-tuning LLMs in Sinhala has gained significant challenges. With a focus on Sinhala specifically, this systematic review addresses the methodologies and outcomes of adapting large language models for underrepresented languages. The purpose of this review is to synthesize existing research, identify effective strategies, contributions, and improvements, and highlight the challenges and opportunities in this domain. By analyzing various approaches, including data augmentation, transfer learning, cross-lingual transfer, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, adapter tuning, and model adaptation likewise, this review provides a comprehensive and precise idea of the current state of LLM fine-tuning on low-resource languages like Sinhala. The results highlight the importance of using creative methods and collaboration to improve LLM performance and usefulness in linguistic environments with limited resources.

titulo: Quantization-Induced Accuracy Degradation in Small Language Models: A Parametric Scaling Analysis
autores: P. Tripathi; A. Sharma; H. Sharma; V. Singh
venue: 2026 16th International Conference on Advanced Computer Information Technologies (ACIT)
keywords: Modeling; Quantization (signal); Accuracy; Memory; Cognition; Cognitive systems; Law; Training; Degradation; Hardware; Apple Silicon; Edge Deployment; GPT-Generated Unified Format (GGUF); Inference Efficiency; Large Language Models (LLMs); Post-Training Quantization (PTQ); Scaling Laws; Small Language Models (SLMs)
abstract: Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) enables the deployment of large language models (LLMs) on resourceconstrained edge devices, yet the accuracy-efficiency trade-off for Small Language Models (SLMs, 3 B parameters) remains poorly characterized. In this study, we present a systematic empirical study of quantization effects across the Qwen2.5-Instruct model family (0.5 B, 1.5 B, 3 B) at five GPT-Generated Unified Format (GGUF) precision levels (8-bit to 3-bit) on Apple M3 hardware with Metal GPU acceleration. On evaluating 15 model-quantization configurations on two benchmarks: a.) GSM8K (mathematical reasoning) and b.) ARC-Challenge (science reasoning), we obtain 30 controlled data points. We propose and validate a novel parametric scaling law, $A(P, Q, C)=\alpha \ln (P)+\beta\left(1 e^{-\gamma Q}\right)+\delta C+\epsilon$, which jointly models accuracy as a function of parameter count $P$, quantization bit-width $Q$, and task complexity $C$, achieving effective $\boldsymbol{R}^{\mathbf{2}}=\mathbf{0. 9 2 9}$ with a Leave- One-Out Cross-Validation Mean Absolute Error (LOOCV MAE) of 4.4 percentage points. Our analysis reveals that Q4_K_M preserves accuracy within 1-3 percentage points (pp) of the 8-bit baseline while halving memory; 3-bit quantization causes catastrophic degradation on multi-step reasoning (21 pp) yet remains resilient on classification (3.5 pp); and an ablation confirms degradation is largely task-independent $\left(\boldsymbol{\Delta} \boldsymbol{R}^{\mathbf{2}}=\mathbf{0. 0 0 3}\right)$. We identify 3B-Q4_KM (2 GB, 82.5% accuracy, 26 tok/s) as the Pareto-optimal configuration for fanless edge deployment.

titulo: Investigating the Fine-Tuning of Large Language Models for Indonesian Sentiment Analysis
autores: A. Y. Indrarahmana; P. Janyoi; P. Seresangtakul; S. Kongyoung
venue: 2025 29th International Computer Science and Engineering Conference (ICSEC)
keywords: Computer science; Sentiment analysis; Accuracy; Protocols; Reviews; Large language models; Zero shot learning; Market research; Robustness; Testing; Sentiment analysis; Indonesian; Large Language Models; LoRA; Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning; Zero-shot learning; macro-F1; latency
abstract: Sentiment analysis of user reviews is vital for product evaluation, yet the behavior of large language models (LLMs) in lower-resource languages such as Indonesian remains under-explored. We compare three LLM families (Gemma, Llama, Qwen) against classic RNN baselines (Bi-LSTM, Bi-GRU) on a three-class Indonesian app-review dataset (InfoBMKG, 8,000 reviews) under two settings: zero-shot and LoRA fine-tuning. In the zero-shot setting, a domain-trained Bi-LSTM outperforms all LLMs (macro-F1 0.84), indicating that general pre-training alone is insufficient for this domain. After LoRA fine-tuning, all LLMs improve substantially; Gemma3-4B-it attains an Accuracy of 0.92 and a macro-F1 score of 0.89. Paired, stratified bootstrap testing (B is 10,000; two-sided) with Holm–Bonferroni correction shows that only Gemma3-4B-it achieves a statistically significant macro-F1 gain over Bi-LSTM, while other LLMs exhibit positive but non-significant trends. Despite these gains, Bi-LSTM remains more than 70 times faster under a unified inference protocol, underscoring a practical accuracy-latency trade-off. Overall, LLMs are not uniformly superior to classic deep learning models in this setting; parameter-efficient fine-tuning is key to unlocking LLM performance for Indonesian sentiment analysis. However, deployment choices should balance accuracy targets with latency budgets.

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been extensively researched and used in both academia and industry since the rise in popularity of the Transformer model, which demonstrates excellent performance in AI. However, the computational demands of LLMs are immense, and the energy resources required to run them are often limited. For instance, popular models like GPT-3, with 175 billion parameters and a storage requirement of 350 GB, present significant challenges for deployment on resource-constrained IoT devices and embedded systems. These systems often lack the computational capacity to handle such large models. Quantization, a technique that reduces the precision of model values to a smaller set of discrete values, offers a promising solution by reducing the size of LLMs and accelerating inference. In this research, we provide a comprehensive analysis of quantization techniques within the machine learning field, with a particular focus on their application to LLMs. We begin by exploring the mathematical theory of quantization, followed by a review of common quantization methods and how they are implemented. Furthermore, we examine several prominent quantization methods applied to LLMs, detailing their algorithms and performance outcomes.

abstract: In this study, a text classification system was developed to automatically classify Turkish user reviews based on their rating labels. Both encoder-based BERTurk models and decoder-based Gemma models were utilized, and parameter efficiency in large language models was achieved by applying the LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) method. The effectiveness of the models was examined with varying sizes of the training dataset. Gemma model achieved 69.80% accuracy and 65.56% F1 score with 10.000 training and 2.000 test samples. The same Gemma model achieved 59% accuracy and 55.45% F1 score with 1.000 training and 200 test samples. BERTurk model achieved 74.13% accuracy and 72.17% F1 score with 100.000 training and 20.000 test samples. Additionally, the BERTurk model achieved 66% accuracy and 54.87% F1 score on 1.000 training and 200 test samples. The results of the experiment indicate that model performance varies based on both model size and training data volume, and BERTurk and Gemma models perform well particularly on large datasets.

This paper surveys language-first systems used in daily workflows and outlines enabling methods such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), quantization, and hybrid deployment. Extending prior descriptive reviews, we integrate quantitative comparisons of veterinary LLMs (e.g., PetBERT, VetLLM) and highlight differences between peer-reviewed and industry-reported results. We summarize emerging evidence for diagnostic reasoning, triage accuracy, and record summarization, and discuss practical risks, data quality issues, hallucinations, and governance. A deployment-focused lens links quantization levels to veterinary use cases. We conclude with future opportunities in multimodal integration, predictive analytics, and One Health–aligned governance for safe and effective adoption in animal healthcare.

abstract: Consumers increasingly rely on existing reviews to guide purchasing decisions, yet face significant challenges in extracting actionable insights from vast volumes of unstructured e-commerce feedback. Automated review summarization offers a promising solution, with large language models (LLMs) emerging as powerful tools for this task. This study proposes a dual-phase LLM fine-tuning framework for review summarization, decomposing the process into two phases: (1) pros/cons extraction from individual reviews and (2) summary generation from aggregated features. Leveraging the LoRA adapter, we efficiently adapt Qwen-series LLMs for both phases, achieving domain-specific optimization with minimal computational overhead. Experimental results indicate that LLMs, including Qwen series, demonstrate robust performance in review summarization tasks on review data from Amazon. The Qwen series models adapt well to the dual-phase generation framework, with the 7-billion-parameter variant exhibiting particularly outstanding performance. In Phase I, it achieves significant performance improvements compared to smallerparameter Qwen variants and conventional deep learning models. When integrated with the purification module, this model further delivers optimal effectiveness in Phase II. Moreover, cross-platform validation on multilingual datasets confirms the framework's transferability, when applied to the review dataset from JD.com.

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have changed how computers read and write text. They are trained on vast amounts of data and can provide clear answers and perform multiple tasks. Rather than just expanding these models, researchers have recently begun including tools, retrieval techniques, and step-by-step reasoning. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), tool-using agents like Toolformer and ReAct, and planning techniques like Chain-of-Thought (CoT) and Tree-of-Thought (ToT) are a few examples. Models are made lighter and faster with the use of Mixture of Experts (MoE) and effective fine-tuning techniques such as QLoRA and AWQ. Multiple levels of reasoning that function at varying speeds are added by Hierarchical Reasoning Models (HRMs). This paper gives a clear explanation and comparison of these ideas. Additionally, it examines actual application cases in various Indian fields, including local languages, healthcare, law, education, agriculture, and governance. The study covers the benefits and drawbacks of multiple strategies. The key ideas are: (1) LLMs remain essential as the fundamental language engine; (2) tools and retrieval help in error reduction; and (3) hierarchical plans improve model thinking but increase system complexity. We conclude with suggestions for adapting AI to Indian languages and future research concerns.

titulo: Deployment-Aware Compression of Large Language Models for Edge Intelligence: A System-Level Survey
autores: E. Dritsas; M. Trigka

keywords: Adaptation models; Hardware; Surveys; Random access memory; Memory management; Artificial intelligence; Pipelines; Foundation models; Throughput; Sustainable development; Compression; compiler toolchains; edge artificial intelligence deployment; large language models (LLMs); pruning; quantization
abstract: The deployment of large language models (LLMs) on edge hardware presents multilayered challenges, including compression, compiler behavior, and system-level trade-offs. This survey provides a deployment-centric taxonomy of compression strategies for LLMs under edge constraints, bridging algorithmic methods and practical hardware toolchains. We examine quantization techniques, including posttraining and quantization-aware variants, under precision-scaling regimes and analyze how they interact with operator lowering, kernel fusion, and numerical drift across compilers such as tensor virtual machine, core machine learning, and tensor runtime-LLM. Pruning and distillation approaches are reviewed with an emphasis on their impact on generalization, robustness, and hallucination under tight memory and energy budgets. We highlight the limitations of existing benchmarking suites, including the lack of robustness-aware evaluation, numerical fidelity tracking under low-precision inference, and explicit treatment of compiler-induced latency and energy variability. Case studies across real-world deployment stacks illustrate how system-level constraints translate into concrete deployment bottlenecks in practical edge LLM pipelines. Finally, we identify the open challenges related to continual model adaptation at the edge, privacy-preserving personalization, and secure and reproducible deployment under system constraints. This study provides a structured synthesis of techniques and trade-offs relevant to practitioners, compiler engineers, and hardware vendors pursuing sustainable high-performance edge artificial intelligence.

autores: T. Tasfia; A. K. M. Masum; E. Meyer; F. Cumbo; S. Aygun

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently shown very promising results on medical tasks such as clinical question answering, report summarization, and decision support. However, their high computational cost makes them difficult to use on resource-constrained devices. Quantization reduces model size and enables lightweight deployment, yet the impact of low-bit precision on medical language understanding remains underexplored. In this work, we present a systematic empirical study of low-bit quantization for medical LLMs. We evaluate multiple 2-, 3-, and 4-bit quantization techniques across several medical natural language processing (NLP) benchmarks and report their results on task accuracy, model size, and inference efficiency. Our study focuses on evaluating different quantization methods on medical data rather than device-specific deployment; the findings show that medical LLMs can be compressed without significant performance degradation, making them strong candidates for future edge and mobile healthcare applications.

titulo: A Comprehensive Review of Llm Neural Network Enhancements for Advanced Driving Assistance Systems Through Quantization
autores: S. B; N. V; A. G S ME
venue: 2025 International Conference on Advancements in Smart, Secure and Intelligent Computing (ASSIC)
keywords: Deep learning; Quantization (signal); Accuracy; Reviews; Computational modeling; Large language models; Safety; Complexity theory; Advanced driver assistance systems; Autonomous vehicles; Deep learning; Large Language Models; Advanced Driver Assistance Systems; Quantization; Activation Aware Weight Quantization
abstract: Deep learning models, particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), have shown high degrees of complexity in recent years and have, therefore, made effective quantization techniques necessary. These are very important for the efficient deployment of models into environments of limited resources in autonomous driving and Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS). Quantization is of paramount importance in the field of ADAS, as accuracy directly relates to safety. More importantly, quantization technique advances do allow the design of safety-critical features with higher accuracy in ADAS, such as the brand new Full Self-Driving technology developed by Tesla, whose processing speeds reach over 100 frames per second and with more than 85 % accuracy. This is a survey paper that covers the latest developments in this particular area of operator quantization, which are Gradient-based Post-Training Quantization (GPTQ), Generalized Gradient Update Framework (GGUF), and Adaptive Weight Quantization (AWQ). While memory could be reduced to a low level, performance is not affected at all. Yet, most of the time, it sacrifices the accuracy of the latest advances in quantization, like PTQ or QAT. We review a plethora of advanced quantization techniques to improve both the performance and efficiency of real-world deep learning models. The aim is to demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness achieved when advanced methods of quantization are applied to improve deep learning models for real applications thereby offering insights into promising research opportunities.

titulo: Large Language Models in Power Systems: A Survey on Applications and Fine-Tuning
autores: B. Sun; Y. Yao; H. Yu; H. Ji; G. Song; H. Wang; P. Li
venue: Chinese Journal of Electrical Engineering
keywords: Modeling; Power systems; Tuning; Printing; Training; Large language models; Optimization; Educational institutions; Measurement; Loading; Large language models (LLMs); power vertical domain; parameter-efficient fine-tuning; specialized LLMs
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are promising tools for knowledge representation, reasoning, and decision-making in industrial sectors. The employment of LLM in power systems is receiving increasing attention, but is still limited by the scarcity of domain-specific data, the absence of unified benchmarks, the complexity of integrating heterogeneous data, and strict physical time-varying constraints. This paper presents a focused survey on the applications and fine-tuning techniques of LLMs within power systems. The taxonomy of LLMs is first introduced, covering general foundation LLMs, industry foundation LLMs, domain-specific LLMs, and vertical scenario LLMs. The discussion then addresses the principles, categories of fine-tuning methods, evaluation metrics, and benchmark datasets that support model adaptation. Finally, the current progress, potential applications, and challenges of specialized LLMs in the power sector are examined, with emphasis on hybrid fine-tuning strategies, multimodal data integration, and deployment frameworks designed to ensure secure and reliable power system operation.

titulo: Aspect-Oriented Opinion Extraction with LoRA Fine-Tuning and Prompt
autores: H. Yanagimoto; I. Kisaku; K. Hashimoto

keywords: Deep learning; Vocabulary; Accuracy; Reviews; Large language models; Natural language processing; Computational efficiency; Prompt engineering; Informatics; Testing; Large Language Model; Deep Learning; Prompt engineering; Fine-tuning; Natural language processing
abstract: This paper proposes a system for Aspect-Oriented Opinion Pair Extraction (AOPE) by fine-tuning a pre-trained large language model with LoRA and adjusting prompts. AOPE is a task that extracts users' aspects and their opinions from reviews, requiring a deep understanding of text, especially capturing the dependency structures within reviews. Pre-trained large language models have a high capability for text comprehension, so the goal is to utilize this effectively. However, adapting a pre-trained large language model to a specific task is challenging. Fine-tuning demands substantial computational resources, and generating appropriate prompts for each task is a laborious process. Our proposed method uses LoRA to reduce the computational resources needed for fine-tuning and combines prompts to improve performance. Evaluation experiments demonstrated that combining prompts with fine-tuning improved accuracy. While there are some areas where accuracy is lower than traditional methods, the efficiency in computational resources highlights the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

autores: S. Xu; L. Zhang; L. Zhu; M. Qin; C. Huang

abstract: Power utilities increasingly require natural-language interfaces that can explain customer-service rules while recognising fault and safety conditions. This study aims to evaluate whether domain-specific parameter-efficient fine-tuning improves consultation quality and fault-inquiry performance compared with an untuned large language model (LLM) and few-shot prompting. A quantitative, paired experimental design was implemented using a reproducible synthetic corpus of 2,400 power-customer cases distributed across eight consultation and fault categories. After validation, the corpus was divided into 70% training, 15% validation and 15% testing sets, and three conditions were benchmarked: M1 base LLM, M2 few-shot prompting and M3 domain QLoRA. The simulated benchmark showed that M3 achieved 88.89% classification accuracy, a macro F1-score of 0.886 and a BERTScore F1 of 0.893. It also produced 99.07% safety compliance and a 1.39% hallucination rate, while its improvement over M1 was significant under McNemar's test $(\mathrm{p}<0.001)$; blinded expert agreement was strong (weighted kappa $=0.857)$. The results indicate that domain adaptation can materially improve technical relevance and safety-oriented escalation in this task. Utilities should combine QLoRA adaptation with expert-reviewed response policies and continuous monitoring. The proposed pipeline provides a practical basis for customer-service triage and operator decision support, but it should not autonomously control grid assets. The principal limitation is that the reported results are simulation-based and require confirmation using anonymised operational data and a deployed model.

For example, medical and chemical texts cannot be created by large language models without previous fine-tuning. Generally, this process consumes good amount of memory and computational resources. To address the issue, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) technique was invented, making it possible to train decent large language model on domain-specific datasets. This paper contains review of several existing fine-tuning methods and results of applying PEFT technique to large language model for MRT medical report generation.

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive generalization across many natural language processing tasks. However, the degree to which they can imitate or exceed classical supervised methods for numerical prediction tasks is less established. This paper presents a systematic metric-based evaluation of frontier, open-source and QLoRA fine-tuned LLMS. The aim is to predict price of the products from text-based descriptions from the Amazon Reviews 2023 dataset, and benchmark against traditional supervised regressors. We develop a rigorous experimental pipeline that incorporates data curation, embedding construction, quantization, and ensemble learning. We compare performance across architectures and number of parameters represented. We assess performance using RMSE, R2 and provide resource-cost metrics in the form of inference latency, memory footprint, and quantization-induced degradation. Our results demonstrate that fine-tuned quantized LLMs outperform traditional regressors while offering substantial reductions in computational cost. This study highlights the potential for hybrid architectures in the future in the context of supervised learning.

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have rapidly become essential to the development of multimodal AI, enabling the creation of systems capable of understanding and combining information from text, images, audio, and video. Despite their impressive capabilities, these models are often difficult to implement in practice due to their high processing and memory requirements. Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a promising solution: a large teacher model transfers its knowledge to a smaller student model, creating leaner, faster, and more practical systems without loss of accuracy. This article provides a systematic review of recent work on multimodal KD for LLMs, focusing on both the technical methods and their applications. Based on the PRISMA guidelines, 46 studies published between 2024 and 2025 were analyzed, covering approaches such as the teacher-student framework, parametrically efficient methods like low-rank adaptation (LoRA), pre-trained pipelines, and compression strategies including pruning and quantization. This review highlights that KD offers clear efficiency advantages, but challenges remain in areas such as handling noise or data diversity, reliance on synthetic labels, and evaluation practices often limited to accuracy alone. Applications in healthcare, social media analytics, and audiovisual segmentation demonstrate the potential of KD, but also reveal its shortcomings in terms of robustness and reproducibility. By mapping these methods into a structured taxonomy and identifying their limitations, this review opens prospects for the reproducibility, customization, and scalable implementation of multimodal KD with LLM.

This paper presents a comprehensive empirical study on harnessing pre-trained Large Language Models (LLMs) for generating concrete test cases from natural language requirements given in user stories. We investigate the efficacy of various prompting and alignment techniques, including prompt chaining, few-shot instructions, and agency-based approaches, to facilitate secure on-premises deployment. titulo: Multilingual Large Language Models for Low-Resource Languages: Challenges and Opportunities

abstract: Multilingual large language models (mLLMs) offer a shared backbone that can support many languages, tasks, and domains. In practice, performance is uneven across languages. Low-resource languages often lag due to limited digital corpora, scarce labeled datasets, under-represented scripts, and restricted compute budgets for training and deployment. These constraints can interact: weak token coverage increases sequence length and can degrade lexical modeling; noisy or misidentified text can dominate small corpora. This paper reviews recent progress on multilingual modeling for low-resource settings and highlights a recurring limitation: many studies improve one component (tokenization, synthetic data, retrieval prompting, or parameter-efficient adaptation) without integrating components into an end-to-end, resourceaware workflow that is reproducible under realistic constraints. To address this, we propose MELM4LR, a modular system blueprint for extending mLLMs to low-resource languages via (i) governance-aware data acquisition and quality control, (ii) scriptand morphology-sensitive tokenizer augmentation with careful embedding initialization, (iii) budgeted continual pretraining with balancing to mitigate language dominance, and (iv) efficient task adaptation using parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) coupled with retrieval and synthetic supervision when labels are scarce. We also define an evaluation protocol that measures task quality alongside robustness, safety checks, and cost, enabling practitioners to report trade-offs that matter in low-resource deployments. Across the reviewed literature, improvements are most reliable when vocabulary coverage, data quality, and adaptation efficiency are addressed jointly rather than in isolation. The paper concludes with open directions on multilingual safety evaluation, equitable benchmarking, and community-centered data practices

titulo: Boosting Large Language Model for Speech Synthesis: An Empirical Study
autores: H. Hao; L. Zhou; S. Liu; J. Li; S. Hu; R. Wang; F. Wei

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have made significant advancements in natural language processing and are concurrently extending the language ability to other modalities, such as speech and vision. Nevertheless, most of the previous work focuses on prompting LLMs with perception abilities like auditory comprehension, and the effective approach for augmenting LLMs with speech synthesis capabilities remains ambiguous. In this paper, we conduct a comprehensive empirical exploration of boosting LLMs with the ability to generate speech, by combining pre-trained LLM LLaMA/OPT and text-to-speech synthesis model VALL-E. We compare three integration methods between LLMs and speech synthesis models, including directly fine-tuned LLMs, superposed layers of LLMs and VALL-E, and coupled LLMs and VALL-E using LLMs as a powerful text encoder. Experimental results show that, using LoRA method to fine-tune LLMs directly to boost the speech synthesis capability does not work well, and superposed LLMs and VALL-E can improve the quality of generated speech both in speaker similarity and word error rate (WER). Among these three methods, coupled methods leveraging LLMs as the text encoder can achieve the best performance, making it outperform original speech synthesis models with a consistently better speaker similarity and a significant (10.9%) WER reduction.

abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into medical document classification represents a paradigm shift in clinical natural language processing. This comprehensive review examines the current landscape of LLM applications for classifying diverse medical documents including clinical notes, discharge summaries, and radiology reports. We synthesize findings from 2020-2025 literature, categorizing approaches into four primary methodologies: parameter-efficient fine-tuning techniques, prompt-based learning strategies, hybrid multimodal architectures, and retrieval-augmented generation systems. Our analysis demonstrates that LLMs achieve superior performance on complex classification tasks compared to traditional methods, with particular strengths in few-shot learning and contextual understanding. However, significant challenges persist including hallucination mitigation, privacy preservation, computational efficiency, and clinical workflow integration. Emerging trends indicate promising directions in federated learning, human-in-the-loop systems, and lightweight adaptation methods. This review provides a comprehensive framework for researchers and practitioners, highlighting critical gaps and proposing a research agenda focused on clinical validation, ethical considerations, and sustainable deployment strategies in healthcare settings.

titulo: Physical-Data Dual-Driven Method for Power Scheduling Auxiliary Decision: PDEVR Closed-Loop Framework with Constrained Large Language Model

abstract: As novel power systems featuring high penetration of renewable energy and power-electronic devices continue to expand rapidly, the complexity of grid operation risks has increased significantly. Traditional scheduling auxiliary decision methods often struggle with slow computation speeds and inconsistent preplan quality. Although existing $\mathrm{N}-1 / \mathrm{N}-1-1$ contingency analysis algorithms can accurately identify high-risk scenarios through detailed physical modeling, they continue to face the persistent “last-mile” challenge: converting numerical results into executable preplans that dispatchers can directly apply. In this paper, we propose a physical-data dual-driven framework that tightly integrates N-1/N-1-1 fault anticipation at the physical layer with a constrained large language model at the data-driven layer, enabling automatic preplan generation. Our core innovation positions the LLM as a “physically constrained decision expressor” rather than an independent physical-state reasoner. We introduce a Perception-Decision-Execution-Verification-Review (PDEVR) closed-loop framework that formalizes verification and review as independent modules. For domain adaptation, we employ layered LoRA together with curriculum learning and physics-informed augmentation. Additionally, our LLM + RAG dual verification integrates over 200 regulations and $5000+$ historical cases, achieving 99.9% compliance in tested scenarios. Experiments conducted on a real 200 -node provincial grid show that our method delivers $8.75 \times$ faster preplan generation time, 98 % completeness, and 94 % accuracy. Overall, we believe this approach opens a promising new paradigm for intelligent dispatching.
